# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

Our new memory allocator (jf2) reduced the 99th-percentile latency of the kestrel key-value store by 59%. Throughput and median latency changed by less than 1%. The 5.7 GB (9.3%) rise in memory use still needs approval from the capacity team.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store. It is the program under test.
- **jemalloc**: an open-source memory allocator library. kestrel currently uses version 5.3.
- **jf2**: our fork (modified copy) of jemalloc.
- **YCSB**: the Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard load test for key-value stores.
- **ycsb-b**: the read-mostly YCSB workload. The standard mix is 95% reads and 5% updates.
- **ycsb-a**: the write-heavy YCSB workload. The standard mix is 50% reads and 50% updates.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish faster than the p99 value. p50 is the median.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **RSS**: resident set size. It is the physical memory that the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the step where jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.
- **NUMA pinning**: NUMA means non-uniform memory access. Pinning binds a process to the cores and memory of one socket.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.
- **Flag**: a configuration switch that turns a feature on or off.

## Test setup

- **Goal**: check whether jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.
- **Host**: bench-07 has 2 Xeon processors with 32 cores each and 512 GB of memory. It runs Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load**: the load average before the runs was 0.4 (nearly idle for 64 cores).
- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of the main branch with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2.
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Run plan**: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run. The builds alternated (A, B, A, B, ...).
- **Reported values**: the median of the 5 runs, with the minimum and maximum.

## Results

The chart shows p99 and p99.9 latency as the median of 5 runs. A is jemalloc 5.3. B is jf2. Lower latency is on the left.

```
          0         2000      4000      6000      8000      10000 us
          |---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
p99           B------A  59% lower
              870    2140
p99.9                     B--------------------------------A
                          3100          68% lower          9800
```

Only the high percentiles changed. Throughput and p50 changed by less than 1%.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 (-59%) |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 (-68%) |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) |

The minimum and maximum of the 5 runs are in parentheses. The notes give one RSS value per build, without a range.

## What the data shows

- **High-percentile latency is lower with jf2.**
  - p99 fell by 59%, from 2140 us to 870 us [Ref1].
  - p99.9 fell by 68%, from 9800 us to 3100 us [Ref1].
  - For both metrics, the highest B value is below the lowest A value [Ref1].
- **The variation between runs is smaller with jf2.**
  - The p99 range for A is 720 us wide (1890 to 2610 us) [Ref1].
  - The p99 range for B is 120 us wide (820 to 940 us) [Ref1].
- **Throughput and p50 did not change measurably.**
  - Throughput was 412 kops/s for A and 409 kops/s for B (0.7% lower) [Ref1].
  - p50 was 118 us for A and 119 us for B (0.8% higher) [Ref1].
  - Both differences are smaller than the range between runs of one build [Ref1].
- **Memory use is higher with jf2.**
  - RSS at the end of the run was 61.2 GB for A and 66.9 GB for B [Ref1].
  - The increase is 5.7 GB (9.3%).
  - Insufficient data: the notes give no minimum and maximum for RSS. The RSS value of each run would resolve this.
- **The spikes in build A occur together with the decay purge.**
  - The spikes in A occur at the same times as the jemalloc decay purge [Ref2].
  - In the spike time windows, 31% of the perf samples are in `je_arena_decay` (a jemalloc purge function) [Ref2].
  - Build B runs the purge in a background thread [Ref2].
  - These observations are consistent with the purge as the cause of the spikes.

## Deviation from the plan

- **Event**: run 3 of build B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
- **Cause**: a nightly scheduled job (logrotate, which archives log files). The allocator was not the cause [Ref3].
- **Action**: the run was repeated. The B results use the repeated run [Ref3].

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload)
- more than 64 client threads
- NUMA pinning

So the results apply only to ycsb-b at 64 client threads without NUMA pinning.

## Open decision

- **Question**: is an RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable?
- **Owner**: the capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 behind a flag in staging.

## References

- [Ref1] Result table in the raw test notes of 2026-11-20 (bench-07, ycsb-b, 5 runs per build).
- [Ref2] perf observation in the same notes (build A, spike time windows).
- [Ref3] Entry for run 3 of build B in the same notes.

---

Notes on this draft (not part of the report):

- **Computed by me**: the percentages and the range widths, from your numbers.
- **Added by me**: the standard YCSB mixes (95/5 and 50/50). Remove them if your configuration differs.
- **Date**: "tomorrow" is written as 2026-11-21. That date is a Saturday.
- **Step 3 condition**: your notes say "if ok" before the staging step. I read that as approval from the capacity team only. Change step 3 if the ycsb-a result is also a condition.
